strengths: The PMEB benchmark is a genuinely useful contribution: it consolidates 13–19 tasks across many public pathology datasets into a unified, reformulated evaluation protocol (retrieval, composed retrieval, classification), directly addressing the reproducibility and incomparability problems the authors correctly identify in prior pathology vision-language work. The ablation on sample-size robustness (1,000 vs. 3,000 vs. 5,000 vs. full) provides evidence that the subsampling strategy is sound.

The idea of repurposing an MLLM (LLaVA-NeXT-8B) as a unified embedding extractor for pathology, trained with LoRA + InfoNCE on image-text pairs, is a sensible and timely direction; a single transformer that ingests image+text jointly is a natural answer to the well-known modality-gap and 74-token limitations of CLIP-style dual encoders.

Comparisons are largely controlled: baselines (PLIP, PathCLIP/PathAsst, QuiltNet) are retrained on the same data as the corresponding MLLM4PUE variants, making the same-data comparisons in Tables 2 and 3 meaningful. Gains over same-data baselines are consistent and sizable on several tasks.

The modality-gap analysis (t-SNE + ||Δ||gap metric from Liang et al.) and the embedding-fusion ablation (question-only vs. added embeddings vs. joint prompt, Table 5) are informative; the ablation also partially validates that the composed-retrieval benchmark cannot be solved from text alone, supporting the benchmark's curation quality.
Efficient training recipe (QLoRA, DeepSpeed ZeRO-2, <0.6M pairs) and clear implementation details (batch size, LR, temperature, hardware) support reproducibility of the method.
weaknesses: Potential train/test overlap that is never addressed: MLLM4PUE-Q is trained on Quilt1M and achieves its most dramatic gains (e.g., Recall@5 = 0.475/0.675 vs. ~0.18–0.24 for others) on Quilt-VQA/Quilt-VQA-RED, which are derived from the same Quilt video source as Quilt1M. The composed retrieval training/test captions may literally overlap. Similarly, classification datasets could overlap with Quilt1M/PathCap captions. The paper must audit and report decontamination between training data and PMEB; without this, the headline composed-retrieval results are difficult to trust.

Internal inconsistencies in counting and citations undermine confidence: the abstract claims '16 original tasks drawn from 15 datasets,' Table 1 is captioned '15 original tasks from 14 datasets' while actually listing 19 rows over ~13 distinct datasets, and Figure 1 shows 16 axes. Reference citations are also frequently wrong (PathCLIP cited as [16] in Tables 2/4 but [37] in the text; Fig. 4 cites Arch-PubMed/Arch-Book as [35]; Table 5 cites Quilt-VQA as [12]). These suggest the benchmark statistics and manuscript were not carefully checked.

Methodological novelty is limited: the embedding extraction (summarization prompt, last-token embedding) is essentially E5-V applied to pathology, with LoRA contrastive fine-tuning added; the paper would benefit from a sharper articulation of what is new beyond domain adaptation (e.g., ablations on the prompt design, the LoRA rank, backbone size, or comparison against CONCH-style architectures trained on the same data).

Fairness of baseline configuration is questionable in places: E5-V performs near zero on retrieval, which may indicate a mis-specified evaluation rather than a genuine weakness of that method; all images are resized to 336×336 regardless of baselines' native training resolution; and composed retrieval baselines only get naive 'add embedding' fusion, while the proposed model gets a tailored prompt — Table 5 shows this prompt mechanism alone drives much of the gain.

No variance, confidence intervals, or significance testing across repeated runs; random sampling of 1,000 benchmark items introduces variance that is quantified only indirectly via the sample-size ablation.

No released code/benchmark artifacts are explicitly promised in the manuscript, which is critical for a benchmark-paper contribution; no limitations or societal/clinical-impact discussion is provided despite the medical domain.

Missing standard efficiency reporting: an 8B MLLM is far costlier at inference than CLIP-scale encoders; the practical trade-off of the 'universal embedding' claim is not quantified (latency/memory vs. accuracy).

strengths: The PMEB benchmark is a useful community contribution: it consolidates 15 tasks from 14 public pathology datasets into three meta-task categories (retrieval, composed retrieval, classification) with a unified protocol, addressing the real problem of incomparable, non-reproducible evaluations in pathology vision-language work. The ablation on subsample robustness (1,000 vs. 3,000 vs. 5,000 vs. full samples) is a sensible validation of the benchmark design.

The idea of using an MLLM (LLaVA-NeXT-8B) with summarization prompts to produce a unified multimodal embedding is a reasonable and sensible direction, and the composed-retrieval meta-task (image+question query) is a genuinely new evaluation setting for pathology embeddings that CLIP-style dual encoders handle poorly.

The evaluation controls for training data by comparing against CLIP-based models (PLIP, PathCLIP, QuiltNet) trained on the same corpora, which makes the core comparison fairer than many pathology foundation-model papers. The modality-gap analysis (Liang et al.) and the fusion ablation (Table 5) provide some insight into why MLLM-based fusion helps.
Results show consistent improvement over same-data CLIP baselines across most classification and retrieval tasks, and the paper is generally well-organized and readable.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty. The core recipe—prompt an MLLM with 'Summarize the above in one word', take the last-token embedding, fine-tune with LoRA and InfoNCE—is directly lifted from E5-V [18]. The claimed 'first time' to use MLLMs for embeddings ignores E5-V, which is cited and even evaluated as a baseline; the pathology-specific delta is essentially domain fine-tuning with LoRA. The paper is better framed as an adaptation/benchmark study than a novel method, but it is not framed that way.

Strong signs of train-test contamination in the flagship result. The composed-retrieval benchmark (Quilt-VQA / Quilt-VQA-RED) is derived from Quilt-1M [35], yet MLLM4PUE-Q is trained on Quilt1M and shows a suspiciously outsized jump (Recall@5 of 0.475/0.675 vs. ~0.2 for all other models, and a large leap even over MLLM4PUE's own 'add embedding' ablation). The paper does not discuss or check overlap between training pairs and VQA-derived evaluation queries. This undermines the headline composed-retrieval claim.

The paper evaluates almost exclusively on its own benchmark, and part of that benchmark (Quilt-VQA) overlaps with its own training data—circularity that weakens the 'universal embedding' claim. No external, established pathology evaluation (e.g., CONCH's or PLIP's standard zero-shot suites beyond the subsampled tasks here) is reported.

Reproducibility concerns for the benchmark itself: subsets are 'randomly' sampled with no seed or released protocol, and the Quilt-VQA/RED items were 'cleaned' with ChatGPT with no details on prompts, verification, or human review of this medical benchmark data. Reproducibility is claimed as a core contribution but not adequately supported.

Numerous inconsistencies and errors that suggest insufficient care: Table 1 says '15 original tasks from 14 datasets' while the abstract claims '16 tasks from 15 datasets'; citation mix-ups in tables (PathCLIP cited as [16] in Table 2, PathCLIP/QuiltNet both as [16], Arch datasets cited as [35] in Figs. 4-5 and Tables 4-5 when they are [12]); typos such as 'achieves baseline methods' (Fig. 1), 'conservative learning', 'MLMMs', 'differents prompts'. For a paper whose stated goal is standardized, reproducible evaluation, this sloppiness is consequential.

Baseline comparisons are not fully informative: E5-V is evaluated zero-shot with no pathology fine-tuning (trivially weak), and CONCH is dismissed via its larger private dataset while the paper simultaneously claims superiority from its own data choices. There is also no comparison to other recent MLLM-embedding or pathology-VLM approaches beyond these.

Claims about longer-context advantages of MLLMs are made but never substantiated: no experiment isolates the benefit of handling long text versus the unified architecture, and no prompt sensitivity analysis is provided despite the entire method hinging on a single hardcoded prompt.

No analysis of practical cost: an 8B MLLM per-patch embedding is orders of magnitude more expensive than CLIP-like dual encoders for the gigapixel, thousands-of-patches reality of digital pathology; for an 'Applied/Systems'-flavored contribution in pathology this omission is significant. There is also no limitations or societal-impact discussion for a medical domain.

Some gains are modest or mixed (e.g., retrieval gains over PathCLIP are a few points, MLLM4PUE-O loses to PathCLIP on several classification datasets), yet the narrative ('consistently surpassing', 'superiority') overstates the evidence.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and relevant problem: unified multimodal embeddings for pathology, moving beyond CLIP-style separate encoders. Re-purposing MLLMs for universal pathology embeddings is a sensible and relatively unexplored direction, and the framing against E5-V (which requires a domain-specific pretrained LLM) is well motivated.

The PMEB benchmark is a genuine and useful contribution: it aggregates 15 tasks from 14 datasets into a standardized, reformulated evaluation protocol spanning retrieval, composed retrieval, and classification, and includes a new composed-retrieval task (image+question queries) that previous pathology CLIP models cannot natively handle. The ablation on sample size (1,000/3,000/5,000/all) showing stability within 0.01-0.04 wF1 supports the benchmark's practicality.

Experiments are extensive and reasonably controlled: comparisons are matched to training data (MLLM4PUE-O/P/Q vs. PLIP/PathCLIP/QuiltNet on identical datasets), multiple metrics are used, and the retrieval, classification, and composed-retrieval results consistently favor the proposed approach under equal-data conditions.

The ablation on embedding fusion methods (Table 5) is informative: it shows that QuiltNet gains little from adding image embeddings to question-only retrieval, while MLLM4PUE with prompt-based fusion gains substantially, supporting the claim that the benchmark genuinely requires multimodal integration and that the proposed fusion mechanism works.
The modality gap analysis (t-SNE plus the ||Δ||gap metric of Liang et al.) provides quantitative evidence that the MLLM-based approach better aligns image and text embedding spaces than PathCLIP.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is modest. The core method is essentially E5-V's summarization-prompt embedding recipe (last-token embedding + LoRA + InfoNCE) applied to pathology with an existing backbone (LLaVA-NeXT-8B). The contribution is primarily an applied/domain adaptation plus benchmark paper, which is acceptable, but the paper's framing as a novel framework somewhat overstates the methodological advance.

Inconsistencies in the reported benchmark statistics undermine confidence: the abstract claims '16 original tasks drawn from 15 datasets,' Table 1 reports '15 original tasks from 14 datasets,' and the conclusion says 15 tasks. Figure 1 also appears to show additional datasets not in Table 1 (e.g., GCS-100k, Wsss4luad appears in both). Similarly, citation labels are inconsistent (PathCLIP is cited as [37] in text but as [16] in tables; Arch datasets as [12] vs. [35]), suggesting rushed preparation.

Potential data leakage for the composed-retrieval task is not addressed: Quilt-VQA/Quilt-VQA-RED are derived from Quilt1M, and MLLM4PUE-Q (trained on Quilt1M) shows a dramatically larger jump on these tasks (e.g., Recall@5 0.475 vs. 0.239 for the next-best matched model) than on other tasks. The paper should verify and state whether train/test overlap exists; without this, the headline composed-retrieval gains may partly reflect memorization.

No statistical significance testing or variance reporting (e.g., multiple seeds for the random 1,000-sample subsampling) is provided, despite results on subsampled test sets where modest differences between methods are interpreted as improvements.

Reproducibility is unclear: there is no explicit commitment to releasing PMEB, the ChatGPT-based data-cleaning pipeline details, or model checkpoints. Since the benchmark is a central contribution, its public availability and exact curation protocol are essential; without them the claimed standardization benefit is limited.

The evaluation uses a single backbone MLLM (LLaVA-NeXT-8B) and a single training configuration; there is no ablation over backbone choice, LoRA rank, prompt variants, or training scale, so the generality of the framework's design choices is untested.

There is no limitations section or discussion of clinical/societal considerations, which is notable for a medical imaging paper claiming a step toward universal pathology foundation models; zero-shot wF1 values well below expert performance should be contextualized.

Writing quality needs attention: Figure 1's caption states the model 'achieves baseline methods' (presumably 'surpasses'), and Figure 4's caption cites datasets with wrong reference numbers. These, together with the count inconsistencies, indicate the manuscript was not carefully proofread.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly defined new task (Pathology Composed Retrieval) with a formal problem statement, addressing a genuine gap: pathology retrieval models are limited to single-modality queries due to dual-encoder architectures.

Systematic framework (HOMIE) with a sensible two-stage design that explicitly targets task mismatch (text-only retrieval adaptation) and domain mismatch (pathology-specific tuning), incorporating domain-aware elements like stain augmentation/normalization, native-resolution ViT, and a progressive knowledge curriculum.

Comprehensive evaluation: composed retrieval, simple retrieval, and zero-shot tile classification against a broad set of relevant baselines (pathology CLIP-based models and general MLLM-based embedding models), with HOMIE matching or approaching SOTA on traditional tasks and large gains on composed tasks.
The paper claims training on public data only, addressing a practical reproducibility concern relative to private-data models like CONCH.
Qualitative analysis (Fig. 3) and modality-gap visualization (Fig. 4) provide interpretable evidence supporting the claimed mechanism (unified embedding space).

Ablations cover each major component (data filtering, curriculum, stain augmentation, native resolution) and the prompt-guided fusion vs. naive addition comparison isolates the architectural contribution.
weaknesses: Benchmark construction relies heavily on GPT-5 to generate relational texts and rephrase answers; the correctness, difficulty calibration, and annotation quality of these synthetic queries are not validated by pathologists or quantified, and the 'rephrasing to prevent cheating' heuristic is not analyzed in detail.

Potential train/test contamination: the model trains on Quilt-1M, while the composed retrieval evaluation uses Quilt-VQA and Quilt-VQA-RED derived from the same source; the paper does not demonstrate overlap analysis or exclusion, which weakens the composed-retrieval results. Similarly, the claim that CONCH's Pubmedset advantage is 'expected' data overlap is asserted without evidence.

All composed-retrieval comparisons are zero-shot; pathology CLIP baselines use only naive embedding addition, and no baseline is adapted (even lightly) to the composed tasks, so the magnitude of HOMIE's advantage may partly reflect lack of baseline adaptation rather than architectural superiority.

Ablation deltas in Table 5 are small (e.g., HOMIE 53.2 vs. w/o stain 53.1) and reported without variance, seeds, or significance tests; several component claims may be within noise, in tension with the strong language used ('each component is essential').
Single backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) only; no experiments varying the MLLM to show the framework generalizes across backbones, and no comparison of LoRA vs. full fine-tuning choices.

Some benchmark tasks are very small (e.g., Video-to-Text with 244 samples, Image-Text-to-Image with 488), and candidate-set sizes/retrieval difficulty are not reported, making R@k comparisons hard to interpret.

Writing quality needs polish: multiple typos and grammatical errors ('specfic', 'criticals', 'Advenced Avg.', 'This is the a benchmark'), and several figures have small/illegible text (Fig. 1, Fig. 3).
No limitations section, no discussion of clinical/safety implications of a retrieval system intended for clinical decision support, and no analysis of failure cases of HOMIE itself.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: existing pathology vision-language models (CONCH, MUSK, etc.) are locked into dual-encoder architectures and cannot process compositional, interleaved multi-modal queries. Formally defining Pathology Composed Retrieval (PCR) and releasing a benchmark is a useful community contribution.
The system is trained exclusively on public data, which is a meaningful and reproducibility-friendly positioning relative to private-data-trained competitors like CONCH.

The evaluation covers three meta-task families (composed retrieval, simple retrieval, zero-shot tile classification) with a broad set of baselines (11 pathology CLIP-based models and 4 general MLLM-based retrievers), plus ablations of each proposed component (data filtering, curriculum, stain augmentation, native resolution, prompt-guided fusion).

The modality-gap analysis (Figure 4) and qualitative examples provide some insight beyond raw numbers, and the proposed adaptations (stain augmentation, native-resolution ViT, progressive curriculum) are well-motivated for the pathology domain.
weaknesses: Potential train/test contamination undermines the headline claims. The Quilt-VQA and Quilt-VQA-RED evaluation tasks are derived from Quilt-1M, yet 500k filtered Quilt-1M pairs are used in HOMIE's Stage-2 training. Similarly, Bookset and PathCap/PathCLIP data are used both for training and for benchmark construction. The paper dismisses CONCH's Pubmedset advantage as 'probable data overlap' while not applying the same scrutiny to its own training-evaluation overlap, which directly inflates the composed-retrieval numbers.

The core baseline comparison on the new PCR benchmark is structurally unfair. HOMIE is a contrastively trained retrieval model with a 7B MLLM backbone trained on ~2.3M pathology pairs; the strongest baselines are either (a) CLIP-style models forced into parameter-free embedding addition, or (b) general-domain MLLM retrievers that were never fine-tuned on pathology data. The decisive missing experiment is fine-tuning LamRA/GME/E5-V on the same pathology data — without it, the claimed 'overwhelming' advantage conflates domain adaptation with architecture.

'Matches SOTA on traditional retrieval' is overstated. On simple retrieval, HOMIE trails CONCH by a wide margin on Pubmedset (R@1 27.6 vs 50.4) and is middling elsewhere; the alternative explanation (data overlap) is asserted, not evidenced.

Benchmark construction quality and reproducibility concerns: compositional queries and rephrased answers are generated by GPT-5, introducing unverified noise and potential annotation bias; prompts are deferred to supplementary material; several benchmark tasks have very small sample sizes (e.g., 244 video queries, 252 Quilt-VQA-RED), making large reported gaps fragile.

The paper's central framing ('Task Mismatch' / 'Domain Mismatch') is more rhetorical than technical. Stage 1 is essentially a LoRA text-only adaptation following E5-V, and Stage 2 is standard domain fine-tuning with augmentation and curriculum ordering; the methodological novelty beyond existing multimodal embedding work (E5-V, GME, LamRA) is incremental.

Internal inconsistencies in the numbers: Table 5 reports HOMIE's composed-retrieval average as 53.2, but the per-task R@1 values in Tables 2/6 imply a different average (~58.8 including video, ~61.3 excluding it); the basis of the averaging is never stated.

The writing is noticeably below publication standard: repeated grammatical/typographical errors ('high-stops domain', 'pathology specfic', 'This is the a benchmark', 'semantically vector', 'Advenced Avg.', 'w/o stain N/A' labeling in Table 5), which suggests insufficient care and obscures technical details.

Despite heavy clinical framing ('computational consult', clinician trust), there is no pathologist-in-the-loop evaluation, no discussion of failure modes relevant to clinical deployment, and no limitations section; the clinical significance claims are unsupported by any clinical evidence.

Details needed for reproducibility are missing or vague: the filtering threshold λ, video tokenization/processing in the ViT, candidate-set sizes for retrieval evaluation, and how tile classification prompts are constructed are all under-specified.

strengths: Clearly motivated and well-positioned problem definition: the paper identifies a genuine architectural gap (dual-encoder CLIP-style pathology models cannot handle compositional, interleaved queries) and formally defines Pathology Composed Retrieval (PCR), a task that appears novel in the pathology domain.

Solid system contribution: HOMIE's two-stage adaptation (language-only retrieval adaptation followed by pathology-specific tuning with a progressive curriculum, stain augmentation/normalization, and native-resolution processing) is a coherent and well-organized framework for converting a general MLLM into a domain-specific embedding model, built entirely on public data.

Comprehensive evaluation suite: the PCR Benchmark covers composed retrieval (multi-image, image+text, video-to-text), simple retrieval, and zero-shot tile classification across many public sources, and HOMIE's large gains on composed tasks (e.g., +34% R@1 on multi-image to text) alongside competitive simple-retrieval results support the central claim.

Useful supporting analyses: ablations of each pathology-specific component, a fusion-method ablation showing prompt-guided embedding vs. naive addition, qualitative examples, and a modality-gap visualization strengthen the empirical case.
Honest acknowledgment of the one dataset (Pubmedset) where CONCH outperforms, with a plausible data-overlap explanation.
weaknesses: Potential train/test contamination undermines the headline zero-shot claims: the training set includes 500k pairs from Quilt-1M, while the composed test tasks (Quilt-VQA, Quilt-VQA-RED) and the video source (VideoPath/Quilt videos) are derived from the same YouTube pathology videos. The paper does not report an overlap analysis or de-duplication between filtered Quilt-1M training pairs and the VQA/video test sets. This must be addressed for the PCR results to be convincing.

Benchmark construction relies heavily on GPT-5 for generating relational text (image-text to image retrieval) and rephrasing answers (to prevent lexical cheating). This introduces (a) reproducibility concerns, (b) possible LLM knowledge leakage into the benchmark, and (c) unquantified noise; no human expert validation of the generated/rephrased annotations or inter-annotator agreement is reported.

Model scale and capacity are confounded with the method: HOMIE is a 7B-parameter MLLM fine-tuned on ~2.3M curated pairs, compared against much smaller dual-encoder baselines. There is no ablation over backbone scale, and it is unclear how much of the gain comes from the framework vs. simply using a larger, more modern backbone (e.g., Qwen2.5-VL vs. older CLIP encoders).

Ablation gains are modest and inconsistently described: Table 5 shows drops of only 0.4-5.8 points, yet the text calls each result 'significant' without statistical tests or variance estimates; the 'w/o stain N/A' ablation (53.1 vs 53.2) suggests stain augmentation contributes almost nothing, contradicting the framing.

Several technical details are underspecified: how video frames are tokenized/fused, the value of the filtering threshold λ, candidate-set sizes for each retrieval task (which strongly affect R@k), and how the 'parameter-free embedding addition' baseline for CLIP models was constructed—all of which affect reproducibility and fair comparison.

Writing quality needs attention: numerous typos and grammatical errors ('pathology specfic', 'high-stops domain', 'is the a benchmark', 'semantic vector', 'Advenced Avg.'), and citation inconsistencies (e.g., [4] is the Qwen2.5-VL report but is cited for 2D-RoPE/window attention ViT designs).

Clinical framing is strong ('computational consult', decision support) but no clinician-facing evaluation, efficiency/latency analysis, or discussion of retrieval failure modes in a high-stakes medical context is provided; a limitations section is essentially absent.
